cards.explanation: The answer is in a village on the plain of Ono. Sanballat and Geshem say, "Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono." (Nehemiah 6:2) They're two of the enemies pestering Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. A village meeting sounds friendly, friends, but the text says they were planning to harm him.

The answer is False. Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, says it plainly: "But they were planning to harm me." (Nehemiah 6:2) Sanballat and Geshem, two of his enemies, sent a nice invite with a not-nice plan behind it. That's like a free cookie coupon that turns out to be a sales pitch, only a lot more serious.

The answer is that he's doing a great work and can't stop. Nehemiah answers, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?" (Nehemiah 6:3) He's talking to Sanballat and Geshem, two enemies who want him to come down. He doesn't argue or explain his whole life, friends. He gives one reason, the work, and asks one question.

The answer is identical. The text says, "Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, doesn't get louder or fancier. He just repeats himself, four times in a row. I've told myself "just one more cookie" more often than that, and my answers were never identical.

The answer is False, the letter is not sealed. Sanballat's young servant had "…an unsealed letter" in his hand. (Nehemiah 6:5) Sanballat is one of the enemies of Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. The text doesn't tell us why the letter was unsealed, so I'll leave that alone.

The answer is that they're plotting to revolt. Sanballat's letter says, "…you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall." (Nehemiah 6:6) Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, later answers, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) So the revolt story was Sanballat's idea, not the truth.

The answer is king. Sanballat's letter says, "According to these reports, you are to become their king…" (Nehemiah 6:6) It's a charge made to sound serious, and Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, calls it an invention. (Nehemiah 6:8) The word is in the letter, friends, but nothing says it came from Nehemiah.

The answer is Sanballat's own mind. Nehemiah writes back, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) He doesn't go looking for who started it. He tells Sanballat, the enemy who sent the letter, that he made it up himself. Short and to the point, and no meeting required.

The answer is True. Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, says, "For they were all trying to frighten us…" (Nehemiah 6:9) What his enemies said was that the Jews' hands would be weakened in the work and it would never be finished. So all those messages had one aim, friends: to scare.

The answer is that he asks God to strengthen his hands. Right after naming what the enemies were saying, Nehemiah prays, "But now, my God, strengthen my hands." (Nehemiah 6:9) The enemies said the Jews' hands would be weakened, so he asks God for the opposite. It's a short prayer, and I love that it's right in the middle of the story.

The answer is the temple. Shemaiah, a man confined to his house, says to Nehemiah, "Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors…" (Nehemiah 6:10) His warning is that they're coming to kill Nehemiah by night. Notice, friends, he's asking Nehemiah to go inside and shut the doors.

The answer is False. Nehemiah says, "Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!" (Nehemiah 6:11) He says no to Shemaiah, a man confined to his house who had warned him of a plot. He asks two questions and gives one answer. I'd have taken a lot longer to say that, and I'd have asked to think about it.

The answer is that Tobiah and Sanballat hired him. Nehemiah says he realized God had not sent Shemaiah, but "…that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) Tobiah and Sanballat are two of the enemies who opposed Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. So the warning sounded holy, friends, but it was paid for.

The answer is that he would sin and get a bad name. Nehemiah says Shemaiah was hired "…to intimidate me so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me." (Nehemiah 6:13) The plan wasn't just to scare him. It was to get him to do something wrong so they could spoil his name.

The answer is fifty-two. The text says, "So the wall was completed in fifty-two days…" (Nehemiah 6:15) That's the wall around Jerusalem, and it's a little over seven weeks. The verse even gives the date: the twenty-fifth of Elul.

The answer is afraid. The text says, "…all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened…" (Nehemiah 6:16) That was their reaction once all the enemies of Nehemiah heard that the wall of Jerusalem was done. The text says, "…they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God."

The answer is that they realize God did this. The text says the nations were afraid and disheartened "…for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God." (Nehemiah 6:16) The text says they realized it was God's work, and that's why they were shaken. The wall of Jerusalem was finished, friends, and they knew whose hand was in it.

The answer is True. The text says, "For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, since he was a son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah…" (Nehemiah 6:18) Tobiah was one of the enemies of Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, and yet he had ties inside Judah. The text gives the oath and the family link as the reason.

The answer is True. Nehemiah says, "…these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah's good deeds, and they relayed my words to him." (Nehemiah 6:19) Tobiah is one of the enemies who opposed Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. The nobles of Judah told Nehemiah about his good deeds and passed Nehemiah's words on to him.

The answer is to intimidate him. The verse ends, "And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me." (Nehemiah 6:19) The nobles were praising Tobiah to Nehemiah, but Tobiah's own letters were meant to scare him. The story isn't done yet, friends, so keep your oven mitts on.
